Chapter 2: Unlearning the Need to Please and Setting Boundaries
As we get older, have you noticed how that urge to seek approval turns into a full-blown habit of people-pleasing? It’s not just about appearances anymore. Suddenly, it’s saying yes when you’d rather say no, putting everyone else’s needs ahead of your own, or shrinking back just to keep the peace. And honestly, this pattern shows up a lot—especially for women. From a young age, so many of us are taught that being agreeable, accommodating, and easygoing is some kind of virtue. Picture this: you’re running on empty, but you still agree to help a friend move. Or maybe at work, someone says something out of line, and you just laugh it off—because you don’t want to be labeled as difficult. These little moments of self-sacrifice might seem harmless, but over time, they pile up. The real cost? It often sneaks up on you in the form of quiet resentment, burnout, or that nagging feeling you’ve lost touch with what you actually want. For a lot of us, the very thought of setting boundaries feels wrong—almost selfish. There’s this fear: What if people think I’m rude, or ungrateful, or just plain mean? Maybe you can remember being told as a kid, “Be nice” or “Don’t make a fuss.” Those lessons stick, don’t they? And before you know it, you’re living your life tiptoeing around others, always careful not to rock the boat. But eventually, something’s got to give. Maybe it’s a friendship that feels totally one-sided. Or a job that just takes and takes. Or even a relationship where your needs never seem to matter. And then it hits you: always putting others first doesn’t actually make you happy. It just leaves you drained and resentful. Here’s the thing—learning to set boundaries isn’t some grand, one-time event. It’s a process. It starts with the tiniest steps: saying no to an invite you’re not up for, asking for help when you need it, or finally speaking up when something doesn’t sit right. At first, it feels uncomfortable—maybe even scary. You might worry about losing friends, letting down your family, or being judged. But as you advocate for yourself—little by little—your confidence grows. Let me share a quick story. There was someone who always picked up late-night calls from a friend in crisis, even when it meant losing sleep or falling behind at work. After a particularly tough week, they let the call go to voicemail. The guilt was instant—but so was the relief. And you know what? The next morning, the world was still spinning. The friend found help somewhere else, and life just moved on.
Stories like this point to a simple truth: boundaries aren’t about shutting people out. They’re about protecting your own well-being. They actually create room for real connection, not just relationships built on obligation or resentment. Most folks don’t realize that saying no can actually make relationships stronger—more honest, more balanced. Of course, not everyone loves it when you start setting boundaries. Some people push back, call you selfish, or try to guilt you into doing things their way. But honestly, that resistance is a big clue: the old dynamic probably wasn’t fair to begin with. It takes real courage to hold your ground, especially when you’re met with anger or disappointment. Over time, setting boundaries stops feeling like you’re building walls. Instead, it starts to feel like self-respect. It’s your way of saying, “Hey, my needs matter, too.” This shift doesn’t happen overnight—and yeah, setbacks are totally normal. But each time you advocate for yourself, you gain a sense of empowerment that people-pleasing could never deliver.
